power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: From early childhood, we form self-beliefs about where we belong, what we are good at, or who loves us.
Despite extensive psychological research on self-beliefs, the fundamental question of how they initially form has received surprisingly little attention.
Existing work on self-belief updating overlooks two critical limitations.
First, it treats self-related learning as arising from isolated events, ignoring that self-beliefs typically emerge from sequences of meaningfully connected experiences.

Second, because updating paradigms operate in familiar domains, participants already hold precise prior beliefs intertwined with established motives and emotional states making it impossible to study belief formation from a genuinely uninformed starting point.

We propose that studying novel experiential domains addresses both problems: individuals enter such domains with neutral, imprecise self-beliefs, enabling formation of "artificial" self-beliefs through repeated feedback in a controlled setting.
As a concrete implementation, we introduce the Learning Of Own Performance (LOOP) task, in which participants form beliefs about their abilities in a novel performance domain.
Extensions of this approach could illuminate broader aspects of self-belief formation, including personality and identity.
This Perspective bridges psychology, computational neuroscience, and sociology around a foundational question: how do we come to think about ourselves the way we do?
Beliefs about "who we are" are fundamental to human existence.
The topic of self-belief is, unsurprisingly, one of psychology's most intensively studied areas (Oyserman, 2007).
text.formatted: The topic of self-belief is, unsurprisingly, one of psychology's most intensively studied areas <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Oyserman, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: While beliefs about who we are in terms of our preferences, abilities, or attitudes tend to be conscious, people are rather poor at knowing how they arrived at that knowledge (Hogg & Vaughan, 2017; Kube & Rozenkrantz, 2021; Markus & Wurf, 1987; Nisbett & Wilson, 1977).
text.formatted: While beliefs about who we are in terms of our preferences, abilities, or attitudes tend to be conscious, people are rather poor at knowing how they arrived at that knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Hogg & Vaughan, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Kube & Rozenkrantz, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Markus & Wurf, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Nisbett & Wilson, 1977)</ref>.

text.text: The same contrast applies to psychological research on self-beliefs.

This literature is vast, covering questions about the nature and function of self-beliefs, their effects on affect, behavior, and cognition, and traces their developmental origins, malleability, accessibility, cultural embeddedness, neural bases, and clinical implications.
Yet a mechanistic description of how self-beliefs are initially formed is missing.
Current approaches offer insight into updating specific, pre-existing beliefs about discrete self-related events, such as how likely it is that I will catch a given disease (Sharot, 2011).
text.formatted: Current approaches offer insight into updating specific, pre-existing beliefs about discrete self-related events, such as how likely it is that I will catch a given disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Sharot, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: They do not, however, explain the formation of self-beliefs, that is, how someone comes to think of themselves as 'a generally healthy person'.
As we will argue, the distinction between belief updating and belief formation has significant conceptual and empirical implications.

In this Perspective, we present a new framework to guide the investigation of self-belief formation and show how this conceptual turn reshapes one of psychology's most key questions: how people come to believe who they are.
Beliefs can be described as subjective representations of aspects of the world and of aspects of oneself (Connors & Halligan, 2014; Stephens & Graham, 2004) (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: Beliefs can be described as subjective representations of aspects of the world and of aspects of oneself <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Connors & Halligan, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Stephens & Graham, 2004)</ref> (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Beliefs about aspects of the world include, for example, semantic knowledge, stereotypes, political attitudes, religious beliefs, or everyday social knowledge.

Although such world-beliefs may overlap with beliefs about oneself (e.g., the belief "Academics are bad at practical tasks" may overlap with the belief " I am not a hands-on person"), the object of the belief is located in the external world.

On the other hand, self-beliefs are oriented internally and range from beliefs about one's physical constitution (Eil & Rao, 2011) to beliefs about one's identity (Stets & Serpe, 2013), personality (Korn et al., 2012), or ability (Müller-Pinzler et al., 2019), all referring to questions about 'who one is'.
text.formatted: On the other hand, self-beliefs are oriented internally and range from beliefs about one's physical constitution <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Eil & Rao, 2011</ref>) to beliefs about one's identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(Stets & Serpe, 2013)</ref>, personality <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Korn et al., 2012)</ref>, or ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Müller-Pinzler et al., 2019)</ref>, all referring to questions about 'who one is'.

text.text: In this Perspective, we focus on the dynamics of self-belief formation.
Self-beliefs are not fixed, immutable properties that a person simply possesses.
Rather, self-beliefs are the accumulated product of a lifetime of learning.
We conceptualize them as context-dependent, motivated, and emotionally valenced templates through which people construe themselves (Markus & Wurf, 1987; Müller-Pinzler et al., 2022).
text.formatted: We conceptualize them as context-dependent, motivated, and emotionally valenced templates through which people construe themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Markus & Wurf, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Müller-Pinzler et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These are dynamic representations of the self that are continuously shaped by one's own actions and their outcomes, by the reactions of others, and by the broader social world one inhabits.
Crucially, this process never arrives at a fixed endpoint.
Self-beliefs are perpetually recalibrated in response to new experiences and social feedback.

In this way, they function as both the product and the scaffold of self-related learning and thereby constitute an ever-evolving interpretive foundation that shapes how incoming information about the self is processed, and from which new self-beliefs continue to form.
What sets self-belief formation apart from belief formation in general is that the self is not a neutral object to be learned about, but an agent with stakes in the conclusions it reaches.
Self-beliefs have been intensively studied across nearly every field of psychology (Oyserman, 2007), including developmental, educational, social, personality, cognitive, and clinical psychology.
text.formatted: Self-beliefs have been intensively studied across nearly every field of psychology <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Oyserman, 2007)</ref>, including developmental, educational, social, personality, cognitive, and clinical psychology.

text.text: Each subfield brings its own conceptual vocabulary, methods, and theoretical commitments.
Despite this breadth, the questions these traditions have asked converge on several recurring themes: When do self-beliefs emerge, and do they change across the lifespan?
What kinds of self-beliefs matter most for behavior, learning, and mental health?
Why do some self-beliefs persist in the face of contradicting evidence?

In surveying what psychology has learned, we aim not to be comprehensive, but to show that one foundational question cuts across all of these traditions without having been answered, namely how, at the level of specific, moment-to-moment learning episodes, do self-beliefs emerge?
Research in developmental psychology has shown that children develop self-beliefs from an early age, which are initially quite rudimentary and become more differentiated as they grow older.

A necessary prerequisite for the formation of self-beliefs is the ability to perceive one's own body and mind as separate from others -and thus to distinguish oneself from others or the world (Lewis, 1990; Steinbeis, 2016).
text.formatted: A necessary prerequisite for the formation of self-beliefs is the ability to perceive one's own body and mind as separate from others -and thus to distinguish oneself from others or the world <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Lewis, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Steinbeis, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: At around the age of 18 months, when children pass the mirror self-recognition test (Amsterdam, 1972; Lewis & Brooks-Gunn, 1979), children begin to distinguish whether events have their cause in the environment or themselves (Gweon & Schulz, 2011).
text.formatted: At around the age of 18 months, when children pass the mirror self-recognition test <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Amsterdam, 1972;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Lewis & Brooks-Gunn, 1979)</ref>, children begin to distinguish whether events have their cause in the environment or themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Gweon & Schulz, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Later in life, from about the age of 6 years until about the age of 12, children acquire the ability to consider social feedback and develop an understanding of "right" and "wrong" (Shavelson et al., 1976).
text.formatted: Later in life, from about the age of 6 years until about the age of 12, children acquire the ability to consider social feedback and develop an understanding of "right" and "wrong" <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Shavelson et al., 1976)</ref>.

text.text: This understanding of valence is an important prerequisite for the formation of beliefs about one's abilities and associated self-efficacy beliefs.

Adolescence is the stage in which more sophisticated self-beliefs form through interactions with others (Bong & Clark, 1999; Rosenberg, 1979; Shavelson et al., 1976), a process that coincides with the emergence of higher-order generalizations about the self, for example, reasoning from the mastery of various school subjects to the conclusion that one is smart (Harter, 1990).

text.text: In line with this, research in social psychology has shown that self-beliefs do not form in isolation but are actively shaped by the social world.

According to Social Identity Theory (Tajfel, 1978), beliefs about who we are emerge in part through social categorization: people define themselves by their group memberships, and even arbitrary group assignment can generate genuine selfbeliefs about one's characteristics and standing (Tajfel et al., 1971).

text.text: Together, these traditions establish that the social environment is not merely a backdrop against which self-beliefs are formed, but a constitutive element of the formation process itself.
Personality psychology occupies an interesting position with respect to self-beliefs.

The most widely used measures in this tradition are self-report scales such as the Big Five which do not capture personality traits directly but rather what people believe about their own personality (Paulhus & Vazire, 2007).

text.text: This distinction deserves emphasis.

Big Five dimensions (neuroticism, openness, extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness; (Goldberg, 1990; McCrae & Costa, 1999)) describe stable regularities in personality traits that can in principle be measured through self-reports or behavioral observation, but a person's Big Five personality profile and their self-belief about these dimensions are not necessarily identical.

text.text: Yet personality psychology has paid more attention to personality traits as behavioral constructs than to how people come to hold the very beliefs that self-report scales are designed to measure.

Clinical psychology and behavioral psychotherapy have established that dysfunctional self-beliefs are central to the development and maintenance of virtually all mental disorders (Rief et al., 2015), including major depression (Rief and Joormann 2019; Beck 1979), PTSD (Gallagher et al., 2020), social anxiety disorder (Hofmann 2007; Clark and Wells 1995), chronic pain (Atlas & Wager, 2012; Büchel, 2023; Wager et al., 2013), and personality disorders (Poggi et al., 2019).

text.text: While the emergence of dysfunctional self-beliefs is acknowledged in biographical anamnesis and patient-specific case formulation, clinical approaches do not trace their formation mechanistically but focus primarily on how such beliefs can be modified once established, for example through cognitive restructuring, exposure, or narrative techniques.
Finally, cognitive psychology offers the most mechanistically precise account of how people view and evaluate themselves in the moment.

Research on metacognition has shown that confidence, i.e. the momentary self-belief that one's current actions or judgments are correct, reflects a real-time evaluation of one's own cognitive processes and contributes directly to task performance (Balsdon & Philiastides, 2024; Fleming & Daw, 2017; Schulz et al., 2023).

text.text: Importantly, this relationship is bidirectional: local confidence judgments shape global self-beliefs, but global self-beliefs in turn constrain how local performance is interpreted (Van Marcke et al., 2024).

text.text: This local-to-global architecture provides a promising mechanistic framework for understanding how self-beliefs about ability might accumulate across individual episodes of self-evaluation.
Taken together, these fields have assembled a rich picture of what self-beliefs are, when they emerge, or how they vary across individuals and contexts.

Yet they share a notable structural gap: while each tradition acknowledges that self-beliefs are formed at some point, none has provided a moment-to-moment account of the learning dynamics through which a person arrives at a belief about themselves.
Without such an account, we cannot explain why two people exposed to similar feedback arrive at very different self-beliefs, or why once formed beliefs may prove resistant to revision.

In the following sections, we argue that this gap is addressable, but only by distinguishing belief formation from belief updating, and by studying the formation process under conditions where it can be directly observed.

Research in psychology and behavioral neuroscience has been dedicated to the question of how people adjust their existing beliefs about themselves in response to new information, that is, how they update their self-beliefs.

The most widely used paradigm for studying this process draws on trial-by-trial feedback (Sharot et al., 2011;  see Figure 2, top panel): participants estimate the probability of experiencing an adverse or desirable life event (e.g., "I think the likelihood of suffering from cancer during my lifetime is 40%"), are then given the objective base rate for that event, and are finally allowed to adjust their original expectation.

text.text: The procedure continues across a series of independent events (e.g., dying in a car accident, being the victim of a crime).

The difference between a participant's initial estimate and the objective base rate constitutes a prediction error: if the participant estimates their cancer risk at 40% but learns that the base rate is 30%, the prediction error is 10 percentage points.

By comparing initial expectations, objective base rates, and revised expectations across trials, one can measure how participants use these prediction errors to update their beliefs, for instance, in the form of trial-wise learning rates (Eil & Rao, 2011; Kuzmanovic et al., 2016; Lockwood & Klein-Flügge, 2021; Zhang et al., 2020).

A parallel line of work on metacognition points to the level on which self-beliefs are formed, not merely updated.
This research shows that beliefs about one's general competence or ability are not simply read off from single-trial performance.
Instead, they emerge from integrating local evaluations over time into more global self-beliefs (Fleming & Daw, 2017; Rouault et al., 2019; Seow et al., 2021; Wittmann et al., 2016).

text.text: This global metacognitive layer, the sense of 'how good am I, in general, at this?', is where we argue self-belief formation takes place.
These paradigms have proven productive for quantifying how people revise their self-beliefs in response to new evidence, but by design, they cannot address how such beliefs form in the first place.
It is precisely this question that exposes two structural limitations inherent to the updating approach:
The first concerns connectedness.
In the classic belief-updating paradigm, each trial presents a different, unrelated life event.

Participants estimate the likelihood of experiencing a car accident, a diagnosis, a divorce: events that belong to different domains, with no explicit opportunity to "connect the dots" in terms of meaning (see Figure 2).

text.text: Each update is thus a self-contained adjustment of a single estimate.
Because the trials are disconnected, the updates cannot accumulate into a belief about oneself.

Such a global self-belief is a generalization across experiences that share a common referent and relies precisely on the kind of integrative processes that metacognition research has identified as the basis of global self-evaluations.
The belief updating paradigm cannot produce this structure.
The second limitation concerns the status of prior beliefs.
In belief updating studies, participants arrive with well-established beliefs about the events they are asked to evaluate, grounded in lived experience and previous learning episodes.
The paradigm is built around on these priors: it studies updating because participants already hold pre-existing probability estimates of life events, and tracks how these are revised.
Importantly, these prior beliefs are charged emotionally, often linked to feedback on one's efforts, abilities, and personality in the past (Tracy & Robins, 2004).
text.formatted: Importantly, these prior beliefs are charged emotionally, often linked to feedback on one's efforts, abilities, and personality in the past <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Tracy & Robins, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Likewise, initial expectations in well-known domains such as health status, intelligence, or risk of robbery are already shaped by personal motives. (see Box 1).

To understand how self-beliefs emerge, we need a setting in which participants lack strong priors, where formation rather than mere updating becomes possible, and where participants enter the task with minimal motivational and emotional investment.
What, precisely, do we mean by belief formation?

Consider a child entering first grade: although they understand in a general sense that people can be better or worse at schoolwork than others, they have little sense of where they will stand among their classmates (Martinot et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Consider a child entering first grade: although they understand in a general sense that people can be better or worse at schoolwork than others, they have little sense of where they will stand among their classmates <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Martinot et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This is precisely the state in which belief formation begins.

We conceptualize belief formation as a learning process through which a person, starting from a relatively uninformed state, develops increasingly differentiated beliefs about a specific domain of experience.

At the outset, the person can draw on pre-existing global beliefs, such as self-esteem, and on whatever specific beliefs they have already formed about related domains, to generate an initial estimate for the new one.
Belief formation is the process by which that imprecise first estimate becomes something more defined.

This happens gradually, as the person accumulates experiences within the domain, with each graded worksheet, each word of praise or correction from the teacher, and each glance at how classmates are doing adds another piece of information.

Across many such experiences, the child's estimate of where they stand becomes more specific and more certain, until it settles into a belief such as "I am good at math" or "school is not really my thing.
Crucially, this accumulation is not a neutral tallying of evidence.

Each new experience is processed by a person who brings prior knowledge, motives, and emotions to the situation, and these factors substantially shape what is learned (Müller-Pinzler et al., 2022; Zamfir & Dayan, 2022).

text.text: First and foremost, any specific self-belief is contextualized by one's personal learning history, that is, the worldviews, knowledge, and experiences a person has acquired across their lifetime, as well as self-perceived characteristics such as trait anxiety, self-esteem, or optimism.
Together, specific prior and global beliefs anchor the belief formation process and constrain what any resulting posterior belief can look like.
This means that any information encountered in daily life can only be processed through the lens of one's global beliefs and a situation-specific prior (see Figure 3).

text.text: Specifically, the person's cognitive strategies, appraisals of the situation, allocation of attention, and current arousal determine how "objective" information is translated into a subjective representation and ultimately integrated into the self-belief formation process.

Taken together, as self-beliefs are formed over successive, connected experiences, learning about the self is affected in a twofold way: by the specific and global beliefs that anchor the interpretation of new information, and by the emotional states and personal motives that shape attention, appraisal, and the subjective representation of incoming information (see Box 1).
Thus, we refer to such self-beliefs as affected beliefs -beliefs that are both shaped by, and imbued with, affect (Müller-Pinzler et al., 2022).

text.text: To investigate how self-beliefs are formed, it would be desirable to sidestep the confounding influence of strong prior beliefs.
With this goal in mind, we propose that one possibility is to construct artificial self-beliefs and then examine the underlying computations through which people arrive at them.

By "artificial", we mean that the self-belief in question concerns a relatively novel domain of experience, as alluded to above: a belief about an ability, trait, or identity that the person has had little or no occasion to think about before.
Although no domain is entirely free of prior expectations, the domain should ideally be as unrelated as possible to other specific and global beliefs a person already holds.
Pre-existing beliefs will still inform the initial prior, but their influence should be far weaker than in domains where people hold firm beliefs.
We developed the Learning Of Own Performance (LOOP) task (Czekalla et al., 2021 (Czekalla et al., , 2026;; Müller-Pinzler et al., 2019 , 2022) precisely to put this approach into practice.

text.text: The task is built around the construction of artificial self-beliefs: participants learn about their ability in two novel domains (e.g., estimating the weights of animals and the heights of buildings), for which they hold no meaningful prior.
By repeatedly performing the task and receiving performance feedback, the artificial belief about one's ability takes shape. (see Figure 2; lower panel).

The feedback sequence is manipulated so that participants receive predominantly positive feedback in one domain and predominantly negative feedback in the other; a cover story ensures they remain unaware of this manipulation (Czekalla et al., 2021 (Czekalla et al., , 2026;; Müller-Pinzler et al., 2019 , 2022).

text.text: That said, the LOOP task captures belief formation within a given performance domain.

Whether domain-specific learning generalizes to broader global self-beliefs remains an open question that future work could address by pairing LOOP with pre-and post-assessment of global selfperception.
Self-belief formation as realized in the LOOP task thus differs from classic belief updating tasks in two important respects.

First, the trials are inherently connected and allow participants to integrate feedback across trials into a cumulative self-belief, rather than arriving at a set of disconnected probability estimates.

Second, participants begin the task without strong preconceptions about their ability in these novel domains: before the first trial, performance expectations cluster around the 50th percentile and are accompanied by low confidence, which rises as the task progresses (Schröder et al., 2025), indicating that new self-beliefs are formed rather than pre-existing beliefs being revised.

text.text: Because the ability to estimate the weights of animals or the heights of buildings carries little inherent relevance beyond the general wish to perform well, the task is relatively motivationally neutral compared with domains participants have already encountered.
Poor performance therefore does not threaten global self-esteem to the same degree as failure in a domain culturally linked to intelligence or social worth (Chestnut et al., 2018).

text.text: This makes the LOOP task also particularly suitable for studying self-belief formation in samples prone to fear of negative evaluation, who might otherwise avoid or be differently engaged in identity-relevant tasks.
Since its development, the LOOP task has been applied to a range of questions about how selfbeliefs form and why this process differs between individuals.

A first insight the LOOP task affords is that the mechanistic approach makes the belief formation process directly observable: by modeling trial-by-trial updates as a function of prediction errors, individual process variables such as learning rates become quantifiable.
This revealed that self-belief formation is not a symmetric accumulation of evidence.

Participants weighted negative prediction errors more heavily than positive ones when learning about their own performance, a negativity bias that was specific to self-related learning and absent when learning about another person's performance (Müller-Pinzler et al. 2019; Müller-Pinzler et al. 2022).

text.text: The asymmetry in how individual feedback signals are integrated means that the beliefs formed are systematically biased.
How strongly this bias operates depends not only on what is being learned about, but on who is learning and the emotions they bring to the process.
A second insight concerns the emotional and motivational processes that unfold during learning itself.

We found that emotional states arising during the task, such as pride and embarrassment, were related to biased learning about one's own performance, suggesting that self-belief formation is shaped by the affect that incoming feedback elicits, and vice versa (Müller-Pinzler et al., 2022).

text.text: Similarly, causal attributions, i.e., how participants explain their successes and failures during the task, shaped self-belief formation: internal attributions of failure led to more pronounced negative self-belief formation (Mayer et al., 2026).

text.text: Both findings illustrate how motives and emotional states are not merely background factors but active determinants of the self-belief that emerges.
These findings lay the groundwork for applying the paradigm to clinical questions.

We were able to examine self-belief formation in individuals diagnosed with depression and comorbid social anxiety disorder, finding that reduced learning from positive feedback might be a mechanism underlying the formation of maladaptive self-beliefs in this group (Czekalla et al., 2026); see Figure 4).

text.text: In a further application, extending the task to include beliefs about another person's performance alongside one's own, we found that narcissistic personality traits were associated with systematic biases in both self-and other-related belief formation: individuals with higher narcissistic traits showed reduced learning from negative self-related feedback, which is consistent with self-enhancement as a mechanism for maintaining a grandiose self-image.

They also experienced stronger pride, which in turn was linked to reduced learning from negative feedback about others, suggesting that devaluing others, in the sense of actively constructing others as inferior to oneself, serves as a second route to the same goal (Matthiesen et al., under review).

text.text: Finally, artificially constructed self-beliefs can be used to study not only how beliefs form but also how they are subsequently revised.
Once a self-belief has been established, the paradigm can introduce disconfirming feedback to examine how readily it is revised and what moderates that process.

This way, we found that participants were less willing to update their beliefs in response to disconfirming feedback once a belief was established, and that this resistance was linked to the level of confidence built up during formation (Schröder et al., 2025).

text.text: Taken together, these applications show how artificially constructed self-beliefs make it possible to study self-belief formation largely independently of individual learning histories, while still capturing how motives, emotions, and individual differences shape the beliefs that emerge.
The idea of constructing artificial beliefs to study self-belief formation has the potential to extend beyond the domain of ability.
Most directly, it could be applied to personality beliefs such as a person's sense of being an anxious, empathic or a sociable person (Flechsenhar et al., 2022).

text.text: The most theoretically significant extension, however, may be to identity.

Decades of research in the identity development tradition, from Marcia's (1966) influential framework of identity statuses to contemporary work on how adolescents and emerging adults construct self-related beliefs (Crocetti, 2018; Luyckx et al., 2014), has established that identity is actively formed rather than discovered (Schwartz et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Decades of research in the identity development tradition, from <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Marcia's (1966)</ref> influential framework of identity statuses to contemporary work on how adolescents and emerging adults construct self-related beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Crocetti, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Luyckx et al., 2014)</ref>, has established that identity is actively formed rather than discovered <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Schwartz et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: What this tradition has not provided, however, is a processlevel, experimentally tractable account of the learning mechanisms through which specific identity beliefs crystallize.
This is precisely the kind of account that the artificial belief formation approach is designed to produce.

Applying this methodology to identity formation would require identifying novel identity domains in which prior experiences are minimal, and tracing how identity self-beliefs emerge from repeated, connected feedback.

Identity formation, like selfbelief formation in the context of ability, does not occur in a vacuum: prior experiences, knowledge, historical and contextual information, and global beliefs about the self provide the blueprint from which novel identity-related information is evaluated and integrated.
It is emotionally charged and motivationally laden in ways that would make their examination difficult.

Thus, to isolate the basic working principles of identity formation from these influences as neatly as possible, the challenge would be to find novel and neutral identity domains to serve as suitable entry points.

We believe this is a promising direction for future work, one that would connect the experimental precision of the LOOP paradigm to some of the oldest questions in the psychology of the self: the riddle of "who we are" (Oyserman, 2007) or how we became what we are today.

text.text: Beliefs about the self are constructed, not given.
They emerge from sequences of connected experiences, shaped at every step by prior knowledge, emotional states, and personal motives.
The artificial belief formation approach makes this construction process experimentally accessible for the first time.

By situating participants in a novel performance domain where no meaningful prior exists, the LOOP task creates the conditions under which belief formation, rather than mere updating, can be observed directly.

Modeling trial-by-trial learning then makes the underlying process quantifiable: how individual pieces of feedback are weighted, how confidence accumulates, how affect and motivation bend the trajectory of an emerging self-belief.
What results is not just a snapshot of what someone believes, but a mechanistic account of how they came to believe it.
This is what artificial self-beliefs can reveal, and what we believe makes this approach a productive path forward for understanding one of psychology's most fundamental questions.

A common assumption in social cognition research is that individuals integrate information into their beliefs in a way that tends toward an accurate representation of reality (see (Vazire, 2010) for critique to this assumption).

text.text: This account, however, overlooks several factors that affect how "objective" information is perceived and interpreted: prior beliefs (both global and specific) anchor the formation process, while motives and emotional states shape the cognitive strategies, appraisals, allocation of attention, and arousal states through which information becomes subjective representation.
As a result, motives and emotions color the entire process of belief formation, often producing systematically biased self-beliefs.

Importantly, multiple motives are at work simultaneously in both cases, e.g. self-enhancement, self-verification, and accuracy motives can all influence the same belief-formation process (see Box 1) and which tendency dominates depends not on prior belief valence alone but on the broader motivational context and the perceived stakes of the situation (Swann & Bosson, 2010).

text.text: Motives and emotional states play an important role in the extent to which information is sought, reinterpreted, or taken note of at all.
Ultimately, they thus influence how beliefs are formed.
At least four different types of motives are distinguished in the psychological literature that can impact self-belief formation.
First, people have a strong tendency to view themselves in a positive way (Hepper et al., 2010).
text.formatted: First, people have a strong tendency to view themselves in a positive way <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Hepper et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: This self-enhancement motive leads people to seek favorable evaluations and process information with a positivity bias, which includes updating beliefs more strongly after favorable than unfavorable outcomes (Eil & Rao, 2011; Korn et al., 2012; Sharot et al., 2011) or attributing success to personal effort while dismissing negative feedback (Kelley, 1973; Miller & Ross, 1975).
text.formatted: This self-enhancement motive leads people to seek favorable evaluations and process information with a positivity bias, which includes updating beliefs more strongly after favorable than unfavorable outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Eil & Rao, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Korn et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Sharot et al., 2011)</ref> or attributing success to personal effort while dismissing negative feedback <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Kelley, 1973;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Miller & Ross, 1975)</ref>.

text.text: Second, people are motivated to maintain internal consistency (selfverification motive) by aligning how others perceive them with their own self-beliefs (Swann, 1983), even if it means rejecting positive feedback that conflicts with their self-view.
text.formatted: Second, people are motivated to maintain internal consistency (selfverification motive) by aligning how others perceive them with their own self-beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Swann, 1983)</ref>, even if it means rejecting positive feedback that conflicts with their self-view.

text.text: Third, people may also seek accurate self-information to make reliable predictions and reduce uncertainty (Bromberg-Martin & Sharot, 2020; Wurf & Markus, 1991), but this accuracy motive can conflict with the self-verification motive.

text.text: Fourth, people can be motivated to improve themselves (Maslow, 1954).
text.formatted: Fourth, people can be motivated to improve themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Maslow, 1954)</ref>.

text.text: This self-improvement motive may be linked to a negativity bias, particularly in contexts where self-improvement is the primary goal, such as skill acquisition, meaning that negative feedback is processed more readily than positive feedback to refine self-beliefs and enhance abilities (Sedikides & Hepper, 2009).

text.text: Although the systematic evidence for these motivational influences draws largely on belief updating paradigms, there is good reason to expect these dynamics to operate even more strongly during the formation of genuinely new self-beliefs, when uncertainty is highest and the personal stakes of arriving at an accurate selfassessment are greatest.

Emotional states and self-related information processing influence each other recursively, as emotions like fear of failure or embarrassment bias attention toward negative cues (Christianson, 2014; Kaspar & König, 2012), reinforcing negative self-beliefs and perpetuating those emotional states while, conversely, positive emotions such as pride consolidate positive self-views in a similarly self-sustaining loop (Müller-Pinzler et al., 2022).

text.text: Emotional states also interact with motives.

For example, individuals driven by self-enhancement seek positive feedback to boost pride (Williams & DeSteno, 2008), but may avoid performance situations to minimize the risk of negative feedback and embarrassment (Apsler, 1975; Feinberg et al., 2012).

text.text: During the formation of self-beliefs, unlike in isolated updating trials, these motivational and emotional dynamics unfold over time and interact with one another, making them integral to the formation process itself rather than mere background factors.

Prior beliefs, emotional states, and motives impact process of belief formation, which can lead to significant interindividual differences in self-beliefs even when individuals are confronted with identical feedback.

The figure illustrates this with two people, one with a strong positive prior belief about their presenting ability (upper panel) and one with a weak or negative prior (lower panel), but with each receiving the same mixed feedback after a research talk.
The person with positive prior presenting ability self-beliefs is more likely to experience pride and to weight audience reactions in a self-confirming direction.

The person with negative prior presenting ability self-beliefs is more likely to experience embarrassment, to attend selectively to negative cues, and to attribute positive signals externally ('others may just be polite'), resulting in a posterior belief ('I am not good at presenting') that diverges markedly from the first person's interpretation of the same event.
